_readme: Edit this file to change stories and facts. Facts come from the NASA pages in each entry's sources. x and y are marker positions in percent of the map. lat/lon are the landing sites.

machines.name: Apollo 15 science station
machines.label: Apollo 15
machines.type: Crewed lander with rover and ALSEP science station
machines.hook: They drove away. I stayed, and I kept listening.
machines.story:
Hi there! I am the Apollo 15 science station. I live on the Moon. Yes, the Moon! The astronauts left me here in 1971. Then they went home. But I stayed! I stayed and did my job. My job was to listen and feel. I felt for moonquakes. A moonquake is a shake on the Moon, like an earthquake on Earth! I checked the Moon's magnetism. Magnetism is an invisible pull, like a fridge magnet!

I caught dust. I felt the heat coming up from deep inside the Moon. A little generator gave me power. It ran on plutonium. Plutonium is a special rock that makes heat. It kept me going year after year. Then one day in 1977, the people on Earth told me to switch off. And I did. Goodnight, Moon! The lander that brought me here was called Falcon. It landed on 30 July 1971.

It landed at the foot of big mountains called the Apennines, near a long valley called Hadley Rille. Two astronauts came with me. Their names were David Scott and James Irwin. They walked on the Moon three times! All together, they walked for eighteen hours and thirty-five minutes. Wow, that is a long walk! And they drove the first rover that astronauts ever drove on the Moon. It was called a rover.

They drove it 27.9 kilometres all around my home. But they never went more than 5 kilometres away from me. They picked up 77.31 kilograms of Moon rocks and Moon dirt to take home. That is a lot of rocks! And before they left, Scott did a fun trick. He dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time. Can you guess what happened? On Earth, the feather would float down slowly.

But on the Moon there is no air. So both fell at exactly the same speed! Amazing, right? The bottom half of Falcon stayed here with me. It was the launch pad that sent the astronauts home. Before they left, they put a small plaque and a little figure on the ground. It was to remember the explorers who had died before them. After sixty-six hours and fifty-five minutes on the Moon, the top half of Falcon lifted off and carried them home.

Bye-bye, astronauts! My power came from my little plutonium generator. It turned heat into about 70 watts of power. That is not a lot. It is about the same as a light bulb! I sent all my readings home by radio. And I took my orders from Earth. My tools did the listening. A seismometer felt moonquakes. A magnetometer checked magnetism. A dust catcher caught dust. A heat probe felt heat.

And other tools felt the solar wind and the tiny bits floating past me in space. I listened and listened, all day and all night. Everything I felt, I sent home by radio. And the people on Earth learned from it, year after year — until it was time to say goodnight.
facts: The lander Falcon touched down on 30 July 1971 at the foot of the Apennine mountains, near Hadley Rille.
Astronauts David Scott and James Irwin made three moonwalks totaling 18 hours 35 minutes.
It was the first rover driven by astronauts on the Moon. They drove 27.9 km in total and stayed within 5 km of the lander.
They brought back 77.31 kg of rock and soil.
Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on camera. They fell at the same speed in the Moon’s vacuum.
The Falcon's descent stage stayed on the Moon — it was the launch pad that sent the astronauts home.
howItWorked: A plutonium-238 generator turned heat into about 70 watts of electricity.
The station sent data to Earth by radio and took commands from Earth.
Instruments included a seismometer, magnetometer, solar wind spectrometer, ion detector, ion gauge, dust detector and heat flow probe.
machines.ending: Controllers on Earth shut the science station down on 30 September 1977.

machines.name: Spirit
machines.label: Spirit
machines.hook: Opportunity is my twin. We went to Mars to look for old water.
machines.story:
Hi! I am Spirit! Do you want to hear my story? I am a robot. And Opportunity is my twin sister. We are the same robot, made two times! We were both sent to Mars to look for old water. I am a rock detective. That means I study rocks to learn about a place. I landed in a big hole called Gusev Crater on 3 January 2004. A long, long time ago, that hole may have held a lake.

A lake on Mars! I read the rocks there like pages in a book. And the pages said something big: water stayed on Mars for a very long time! I drove 7.7 kilometres across the crater. That is a long drive for a little robot! The Sun gave me power through my solar panels. My solar panels are like big flat wings that drink sunlight. My mast held my cameras up high, like a neck and a head.

My arm reached out and touched the rocks. Touch, touch! My wheels took me where the people on Earth told me to go. They drove me from millions of miles away! Can you believe that? At night, my heaters kept my important parts warm. Brrr, Mars is cold at night! My antenna was my voice. It was how I talked to Earth and listened for their answers. My twin and I landed on opposite sides of Mars.

That means very, very far away from each other! We both hunted for old water, each in our own way. Together, we helped people learn new things about the early days of Mars. My body was a strong shell. It kept my computers safe and warm. My cameras were my eyes. My other tools were my other senses. They told me all about the world around me. Lots of us Mars robots carried a little piece of home with us.

It was art and signs from the people who made us, and from the time we were made. It was like a little hello from home! Every morning, the Sun came up over the edge of the crater. Yay, morning! My panels drank the light, and I woke up again. The people on Earth drove me from far, far away. Every turn I made, someone far away had thought of it first.

I was not fast. I was slow and careful, like a snail. I stopped. I looked. I touched. I moved on. And the rocks told me their story, one tiny grain at a time. Gusev was a quiet place. Shhh! A lake had been here once, long before me. I spent my days looking for where the water had gone. Where did it go? Dust settled on everything. Then the wind blew it away.

Whoosh! And I kept going. My twin was far away, on the other side of Mars. She was doing the same work in her own way. I liked knowing she was out there. Hi, twin! The nights were the hardest. My heaters hummed. Hmmm. My computers slept. And I waited for the Sun to come back. Each sunrise was a new chance to look, to drive, to listen. The rocks I read had waited a very, very long time for someone to read them.

My twin and I found the same answer: water, long ago, on a dry red world. When my wheels stopped, I was still me. I was a listener. I was a reader of rocks. I was a robot who did what she came to do. I never met my twin. But we were the same robot, made two times. Her story and my story are one story, told from two sides of Mars. The end!
facts: Spirit and Opportunity were identical twin rovers.
Spirit landed on 3 January 2004 in Gusev Crater, a possible former lake inside a giant impact crater.
The mission set out to look for signs of past water on Mars.
The rock record showed that water was long standing on Mars’s surface in ancient times.
Spirit traveled 7.7 km (4.8 miles) on Mars.
howItWorked: My mast held cameras like a neck and head, and my robotic arm reached out to touch rocks up close.
Wheels carried me across Mars, and people on Earth drove me from millions of miles away.
machines.ending: I last spoke to Earth on 22 March 2010. NASA kept listening for over a year, and on 25 May 2011 they said my mission was complete.

machines.name: Opportunity
machines.label: Opportunity
machines.hook: I kept going for years past my plan, until a dust storm hid the Sun.
machines.story:
Hi! I am Opportunity! I am a robot who drives on Mars. Vroom, vroom! Well, not so fast. I drive very, very slowly. I landed on a flat place called Meridiani Planum on 24 January 2004. The ground there had special minerals in it. Those minerals only form in wet places. So the ground was telling me a secret: Mars used to be wet! I kept driving and driving and driving.

In all, I drove 45.16 kilometres. That is farther than any robot had ever driven on another world! I was the champion driver of Mars! My driving record stood for years and years. Then Perseverance passed it in October 2026. One day in 2014, I took a picture of myself. Click! I saw that the wind had blown much of the dust off my solar panels. The wind on Mars kept me going!

Thank you, wind! I ran on sunlight. So dust was big trouble for me. If dust covered my panels, the Sun could not reach them. Uh-oh! My mast held my cameras up high, like a neck and a head. My arm reached out and touched the rocks. My wheels carried me across Mars. And the people on Earth drove me from millions of miles away. In the end, I kept going for almost fifteen years!

That is a very long time! I went through dust and cold, long after my planned time was up. What my twin and I found added to what other Mars robots had found. It helped answer the big questions about Mars. Neither of us could have told the whole story alone. My brains were computers. They took in everything I saw and felt. Perseverance passed my mark of 28.06 miles.

And it is still going! Then, in June 2018, a huge dust storm spread across the whole planet. It hid the Sun from my solar panels. Uh-oh! After that, I never got to talk to Earth again. The people who made us put a little piece of themselves into us. It was art and signs from our time and place. We carried it with us on the journey. It was like a little hello from home!

Meridiani was a flat, open place. The ground under my wheels was full of minerals that only form in wet places. The whole plain was a memory of water. I drove farther than any robot had ever driven on another world. Every kilometre was a new page in a book. My panels were my lifeline. The Sun fed them, and they fed me. Yum, sunlight! The people on Earth drove me from millions of miles away.

I went where they pointed me, one slow, careful drive at a time. Slow and steady wins the race! I was not made to hurry. I was made to keep going. And I did! Through dust and cold, season after season. My twin Spirit was on the other side of Mars. She was doing the same work in a different place. She was reading the same old story of water, but from different rocks.

The nights were long. My heaters kept my important parts warm until the Sun came back. Brrr! Dust was my enemy and my friend. It could cover my panels and stop my light. Uh-oh! And the wind could blow it away again. Whee! I had driven 45.16 kilometres. That is farther than any robot before me. And I had found what I came to find. Mars was once a wet world.

And its rocks still remembered the water. Every rock I touched, every picture I took, was a page in the story of a world that was once wet. And that story is still being read today. The end!
facts: Opportunity landed on 24 January 2004 on Meridiani Planum, where mineral deposits suggested a wet past.
It drove 45.16 km (28.06 miles), the off-Earth driving record until Perseverance passed it on 11 October 2026.
It was solar powered.
In a 2014 self-portrait, wind had cleaned much of the dust off its solar panels.
howItWorked: Solar panels powered the rover, so dust and blocked sunlight were serious problems.
My mast held cameras like a neck and head, and my robotic arm reached out to touch rocks up close.
Wheels carried me across Mars, and people on Earth drove me from millions of miles away.
machines.ending: A planet-wide dust storm covered the rover’s location. Opportunity last communicated with Earth on 10 June 2018.

machines.name: Ingenuity
machines.label: Ingenuity
machines.hook: Five flights was the plan. I flew 72.
machines.story:
Hi! I am Ingenuity! I am a little helicopter. I can fly! Whee! I weigh just 1.8 kilograms. That is very, very light! I flew to Mars tucked under a big rover called Perseverance. It was like hiding under a big friend! On 19 April 2021, I did something no one had ever done before. I flew! Up, up, up! It was the first time a machine flew on another planet.

I was only meant to try five short flights in 30 days. Just five! But guess what? I flew 72 times! I flew for almost three years. I flew ahead to look for the rover. I even saw bits of its landing gear on the ground. In all, I flew for about 129 minutes. I flew 17 kilometres. And I climbed as high as 24 metres. All of this in air that is less than one percent as thick as Earth's air!

The air on Mars is super thin, like almost no air at all! Every flight was a big gamble. And I won it seventy-two times! Yay! I launched on 30 July 2020. I landed in a place called Jezero Crater on 18 February 2021. A solar panel charged my batteries. It gave me enough power for about one ninety-second flight each Martian day. Ninety seconds is not long. Count to ninety!

One, two, three... My blades were about 1.2 metres across. They had to spin very, very fast to push against the thin air. Spin, spin, spin! Before I ever flew, I had to live through my first night alone on Mars. It was cold and dark, and I made it! Brrr! On Earth, I weigh 4 pounds. On Mars, I weigh only 1.5 pounds. That is because Mars is smaller than Earth, so it pulls me less!

People called my first flight a Wright Brothers moment. The Wright Brothers were the first people to fly on Earth. And I was the first to fly on Mars! I showed the way for the flying robots that will come after me. I flew for the last time on 18 January 2024. In my last flights, I tried new things. I pushed myself to see how far a little helicopter like me could go.

How high can I go? How fast can I go? I flew higher and faster than anyone had dreamed. Wow! The helicopters that come after me will look for places where people can land. And they will map ice under the ground. By July 2021, I was flying to new places. No helicopter had ever been there before! In August 2021, I saw the rover from the sky. There was my friend, small and bright on the red ground.

Hi, friend! In April 2022, I set my distance record. That same month, I flew over the rover's landing gear. It was lying on the ground where it had fallen. In October 2023, I set my height record. A week later, I set my speed record. I was still getting better! I was still learning new things I could do, more than two years after my first flight. Each new place I flew to was a place no one had ever seen from above.

It was Mars, seen from the sky, for the very first time! Can you imagine seeing Mars from the sky? I was small. And the whole world said a helicopter could not fly on Mars. The air was too thin. The cold was too deep. The odds were too long. But my blades spun fast. Spin, spin, spin! And the thin air held me. And I rose up into the sky!

Whee! The rover watched me from below. And I watched the rover from above. Together, we explored a crater. Neither of us could have explored it alone. We were a team! My first flight was only the start. It was not the end. The helicopters that come after me will fly farther than I ever did. And they will stand on my shoulders. I did not just fly. I showed everyone that the sky of another world is open. And that flying there is possible. I was only a test. And the test became a big win!
facts: Ingenuity launched on 30 July 2020 and landed in Jezero Crater on 18 February 2021.
Its first flight, on 19 April 2021, was the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
The plan was five test flights at most. It completed 72 flights over nearly three years.
It flew about 128.8 minutes, covered 17.0 km and climbed as high as 24.0 m (78.7 ft).
Mars’s atmosphere is less than 1 percent as dense as Earth’s.
howItWorked: A solar panel charged lithium-ion batteries, enough for about one 90-second flight per Martian day.
Its blades span about 1.2 m and had to spin fast to push against very thin air.
machines.ending: Ingenuity flew for the last time on 18 January 2024. NASA completed the mission on 25 January 2024.

machines.name: InSight
machines.label: InSight
machines.hook: I didn't study Mars from above. I listened to its inside.
machines.story:
Hi! I am InSight! Shhh! Listen with me. I am a very good listener. I landed on 26 November 2018 on a flat, smooth plain called Elysium Planitia. It was not picked because it looked exciting. It was picked because it was safe. My work was inside Mars, not on top of it. I have a robot arm. It is 1.8 metres long. That is longer than you are tall!

With it, I put a seismometer and a heat probe down on the ground. Then I listened for marsquakes. What is a marsquake? It is a shake on Mars, like an earthquake on Earth! A seismometer is a tool that feels shakes. A heat probe is a tool that feels warmth. I could even hear the wind on Mars. It rumbled, low and quiet, through my sensors. Whoosh! Two tiny cubesats called MarCO flew to Mars with me.

They were the size of a briefcase! A briefcase is a little bag for papers. They were the first of their kind to travel between planets. The marsquakes I heard are still teaching people today. They found lumps of old crash bits hiding deep inside Mars. On the surface, Mars looks still and quiet. Shhh! But underneath, it shakes, and it is warm. I was the first mission built to explore the deep inside of Mars.

My work had two big goals. I wanted to learn how all the rocky planets were made. I was made to take the planet's vital signs. That means its heartbeat, its warmth, and its reflexes. Thump, thump! Elysium is a funny name. It means paradise in old Greek stories. Paradise is a very happy place! It is the Elysian Fields. And my friend Curiosity lives only 600 kilometres away from me, in a place called Gale Crater.

That is not far at all! I launched on 5 May 2018. I landed near the middle of Mars, where the ground was flat and safe. My work was underneath, not on top. My seismometer felt the shaking of marsquakes. It felt the shakes when space rocks hit the ground, too. Boom! My heat probe felt the warmth coming from inside Mars. My arm lifted both tools from my deck and put them on the ground.

Gently, gently! I studied the deep inside of Mars. It has three parts: the crust, the mantle, and the core. The crust is the outside, like the skin of an apple. The mantle is the middle. The core is the very centre, like the seeds in the middle of the apple! On 1 December 2018, my sensors heard the wind. It was a low rumble. It was blowing at 10 to 15 miles an hour.

I was built like the Phoenix lander. Phoenix was a robot that had already worked on Mars. I launched on a big Atlas V rocket. It took off from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California. The wind I heard matched the dust-devil marks seen from space. What is a dust devil? It is a little whirlwind that leaves marks on the ground! Once my tools were on the ground, my work was to wait.

A lander does not drive. A lander waits. I waited through the cold nights and the dusty days. Brrr! And I listened. I listened to the shaking deep below. I listened to the wind moving over the plain. I listened to the quiet in between. Shhh! The ground spoke in shakes. I wrote down every one of them. And I sent them home to Earth. The heat probe felt the warmth rising from inside the planet.

It was slow and steady. It was the warmth of a world that is still alive. Together, my tools took the vital signs of a whole world. Its heartbeat. Thump, thump! Its warmth. Its reflexes. And they found that Mars is still alive inside. It still shakes. And it is still warm. Elysium was a quiet place. And that was the point. The plain was flat and smooth. The wind moved the dust in long lines.

The Sun rose and set. And I listened. The MarCO cubesats had flown to Mars with me. Then they went their own way. Bye-bye, little friends! And I was alone after that. Alone with the ground and the sky and the shaking deep below. I did not need to move to explore. I only needed to listen, and to feel, and to wait. And the planet told me everything. That is what I was sent to do. And I did it! The end!
facts: InSight launched on 5 May 2018 and landed on 26 November 2018 near the Martian equator.
It studied the deep interior of Mars: crust, mantle and core.
The landing site was picked for safety because the mission studied the inside, not the surface.
Its robotic arm was over 1.8 m (5 ft 9 in) long.
Two small MarCO cubesats launched with it, the first interplanetary cubesats.
Marsquake data later showed lumps of old impact material scattered in the mantle.
howItWorked: A seismometer feels vibrations from marsquakes and meteoroid impacts.
A heat probe measures heat coming from inside Mars.
The robotic arm lifted both instruments from the deck onto the ground.
machines.ending: My last message home was on 15 December 2022. NASA declared my mission over on 21 December 2022.

machines.name: Dawn
machines.label: Dawn
machines.hook: I didn't just visit two worlds. I stayed with both of them.
machines.story:
Hi! I am Dawn! I am a space traveller. I love to travel far, far away!

I was NASA’s first truly interplanetary spaceship. Wow, that is a big word! It means a spaceship that goes to more than one world and stays a while at each. I set off on 27 September 2007.

I flew out to the main asteroid belt. It is a ring of rocky worlds between Mars and Jupiter. And I did not just fly past. No, no! I stayed a long while with two very different neighbours.

One is Vesta, a giant asteroid. The other is Ceres, a dwarf planet with bright spots on its face. What is a dwarf planet? It is a round world that circles the Sun but is smaller than a planet!

I am an orbiter. That means I fly in circles around a world. Round and round I go! I flew in circles around Vesta for a long stay. Then I travelled on and flew in circles around Ceres.

People on Earth could follow my whole journey on a computer. It was built from my real mission data. They could watch me travel from Earth to the belt, step by step.

NASA says my mission was a success! Yay! I did not just visit two worlds. I stayed with both. And staying is how you learn a place.
facts: Dawn launched on 27 September 2007.
It had extended stays at the giant asteroid Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres.
Both live in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
NASA lists the mission as successful.
howItWorked: Dawn was an orbiter — it circled Vesta for a long stay, then travelled on and circled Ceres.
It was NASA's first truly interplanetary spaceship, built to visit more than one world.
machines.ending: NASA lists Dawn as a successful mission.

machines.name: NEAR Shoemaker
machines.label: NEAR Shoemaker
machines.hook: Landing was never part of my job. I did it anyway.
machines.story:
Hi! I am NEAR Shoemaker. That is a long name! You can call me NEAR. My job was to fly in circles around an asteroid named Eros. What is an asteroid? It is a big rock that flies around the Sun. Round and round it goes! On the way there, I flew past another asteroid. Its name was Mathilde. That was in 1997. In February 2000, I became the first human-made thing ever to fly in circles around an asteroid!

Yay! I was the very first! But I got there about a year late. Uh-oh! An engine burn went wrong on the way. An engine burn is when a robot fires its engine to change where it is going. It is like a big push! Then, on 12 February 2001, I floated gently down and touched the ground. I was going only about 6.4 kilometres an hour. That is slower than a person on a bike!

Nobody had planned for me to land at all. But I made it! Hooray! And I kept sending data back for about two more weeks. Then the cold out there finally made me quiet. Brrr! In the end, I sent back about ten times more data than planned. That included 160,000 pictures of Eros! Wow, that is a lot of pictures! I came to Eros to fly around it, not to touch it.

But in the end, touching it was my best moment. After I went quiet on 28 February 2001, the people on Earth tried to call me one more time, on 10 December 2002. Hello? Hello? But I never answered. Those 160,000 pictures were my gift back to Earth. They showed Eros up close, for the very first time! On the way, I swung past Earth itself. I used Earth to give me a big push.

Whee! I flew just 540 kilometres above home! That is close! A month after I reached orbit around Eros, NASA gave me a second name. My new name was Shoemaker. It was for Eugene Shoemaker. He was a geologist who studied asteroids. What is a geologist? It is a person who studies rocks. On the way down, I took 69 close-up photos of Eros. Click, click, click! I was the first mission of NASA's Discovery program.

It is a program for small, low-cost missions. Low-cost means it does not cost a lot of money. They are picked in a contest. And I won! I launched on 17 February 1996. My solar cells kept me going, even far away from the Sun, past the orbit of Mars. I was the first spaceship to run on sunlight that far out. My tools were a camera, an infrared eye, a laser that measured distances, and a magnetometer.

What is a magnetometer? It is a tool that checks for a magnetic field. A magnetic field is an invisible pull, like a fridge magnet! They found that Eros has no magnetic field at all. And Eros is about 21 miles long. I weigh 805 kilograms. That is very heavy! I launched on a Delta rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida, on 17 February 1996. Eros was 355 million kilometres from Earth.

That is a very, very, VERY long way to go for a small robot! My goal was to learn everything about Eros. What was it made of? What shape was it? How was its weight spread inside? And did it have a magnetic field? So many questions! On the way, I flew past the asteroid Mathilde on 27 June 1997. The flyby lasted just 25 minutes. That is very quick!

I got close enough to take pictures of 60 percent of it. Mathilde was 4.5 billion years old. That is older than anything you can imagine! It was covered in craters. A crater is a big round hole. And it was lighter than anyone had thought. My first flyby of Eros was on 23 December 1998. It showed that Eros was smaller than people had thought. It had two craters and one long ridge.

What is a ridge? It is a long, high line on the ground, like a hill that goes on and on. And Eros was as dense as Earth's crust. That means it was packed as tightly as the outside of Earth. I flew in circles around Eros for almost a year before I came down. I dipped as low as 5 kilometres above the ground to look closer. That is very close!

And I mapped more than 70 percent of it. I carried six tools. Each one was like a sense. A camera to see. An infrared eye to feel heat. A laser to measure distance. A magnetometer to check for a magnetic field. An X-ray eye to read the rocks. And a radio tool to weigh Eros from the inside. Flying in circles was my job. Landing was never in the plan. And yet the landing is what everyone remembers! The end!
facts: NEAR launched on 17 February 1996 and flew past asteroid Mathilde on 27 June 1997.
An aborted engine burn in December 1998 delayed the Eros rendezvous by about a year.
It entered orbit around Eros on 14 February 2000, a first for any human-made object.
It touched down on Eros on 12 February 2001 at about 6.4 km/h, the first landing on an asteroid.
It returned about 10 times more data than planned, including 160,000 images.
Eros has no magnetic field and is about 21 miles long.
howItWorked: Solar cells powered it beyond Mars’s orbit, a first for a spacecraft.
Its instruments included a camera, an infrared spectrometer, a laser rangefinder and a magnetometer.
machines.ending: Last contact was on 28 February 2001. The spacecraft succumbed to extreme cold of about minus 173 degrees C.
machines.nowAt: On the surface of asteroid 433 Eros, near a saddle-shaped feature called Himeros.
